messages.subject: Test statistics in mediated relationships in lavaan
parts:
Hi there,

I am an applied researcher, and I have a small question about test statistics especially b, standard errors & z-values that lavaan produces if a researcher is interested in testing mediation. My understanding is that, the product of two paths in a simple mediated relationship does not follow a normal distribution (according to recent publications of Andrew F. Hayes) and that the only way to tell if a mediated relationship is significant or not is by using confidence intervals. However, I am wondering lavaan does produce these statistics and I don't know if they are reliable or not (I guess they are reliable but I am a little confused). A clarification would be highly appreciated.

Thanks,

Pita

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: Test statistics in mediated relationships in lavaan
parts:
Pita

You are correct, it cannot be assumed that the a*b term is normally distributed, but this is not new, there is a lot of literature about it.

Now, in lavaan if you do the analysis with the default features, this would lead to what is called the sobel test. Which means that the inference is made with the wald test assuming the product term is normally distributed.

There are mainly 2 ways that are recommended to deal with this, (a) use bootstrap Confidence Intervals and standard errors as bootstrap does not assume the parameter is normally distributed, for example

mod_med <- '
shs ~ cp*ple + b*grat
grat ~ a*ple

## indirect
ind := a*b
tot := a*b + cp ## total
'

fit_med_boot <- sem(mod_med, data=dat, meanstructure=T,fixed.x=F,
                    se="bootstrap", bootstrap=5000, verbose=T)
summary(fit_med_boot, standardize=T, rsquare=T)
parameterestimates(fit_med_boot, boot.ci.type="bca.simple",
                   level=0.95, standardize=T,
                   zstat = F, pvalue = F)

the second option (b) is to use the montecarlo simulation approach which is available with a function from semTools, like this

exp_ind <- 'a*b'
exp_tot <- 'a*b + cp'

mont_ind <- monteCarloMed(exp_ind, object = fit_med_sobel,
                          plot=T, CI=95)
mont_ind

mont_tot <- monteCarloMed(exp_tot, object = fit_med_sobel,
                          plot=T, CI=95)
mont_tot

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Test statistics in mediated relationships in lavaan
parts: Sobel test has suffered and probably succumbed to a lot of criticisms.

FYI, lavaan does not provide the Sobel test.  The Sobel test assumes that a and b have uncorrelated sampling distributions.  lavaan uses the delta method, which takes that correlation into account.  So it will work better than the Sobel test regardless, and the delta method yields nominal Type I error rates in sufficiently large samples.  The Monte Carlo method Mauricio mentioned is much less computationally intensive and works about as well as bootstrapping in smaller samples (but both break in small samples, for different reasons).

parts:
Hi, Harmanjit.

Q1. It's a good question, but the answer is that it doesn't matter. The adjustments in MLR are to the standard errors, not the point estimates. The bootstrapped confidence intervals do not rely on the standard errors.

Q2. The total effect is a derived quantity (direct + indirect) that is often of substantive interest (X  on Y regardless of path to get there), but is not in itself part of the estimated model.

Pat

messages.subject: Re: Test statistics in mediated relationships in lavaan
parts: Query 1: If there is no missing data, but data is non=normal, and we are using robust estimators like MLM in sem() to contain non-normalcy of data; then should we prefer montecarlo method to bootstrap method (since bootstrap does not run with MLR or MLM estimators)?

If you requested robust SEs, then the Monte Carlo method for CIs will use the robust sampling covariance matrix, returned by the vcov() method, so yes, nonnormality will be accounted for.  In sufficiently large samples (depends how large your model is), Monte Carlo and bootstrapping should yield the same results, but Monte Carlo would not be computationally intensive, so you would get your answer in a couple seconds instead of a couple minutes.  Regardless of industry standards, you can cite the paper on the monteCarloMed() help page to support your choice.  From what I have observed, the hype about bootstrapping tends to be based on minute differences in small samples.

Note that in the development version of semTools, monteCarloMed() is replaced by monteCarloCI() because it is a more general method than simply for mediation models.  Also, you also have the option of simply passing your fitted lavaan model with user-defined parameters, so the function will automatically detect those and return CIs for all user-defined parameters.

devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Did you install semTools in a fresh R session, so it did not conflict with a previously installed version?  That could be a problem if the old version is currently loaded or even just in the PATH.  You can check sessionInfo() to verify semTools is not currently loaded before installing.  Sometimes it is also necessary to shut R down and restart it before loading the development version of the semTools library.
